messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sokha is a 60-year-old Cambodian American man who has worked for years as a hotel manager, a role he once valued because he knew how to keep a busy building calm and orderly. The event that still organizes his life began during a maintenance emergency at the hotel, when a cleaning chemical was accidentally mixed in a poorly ventilated service area. He remembers the sharp, acrid taste that hit the back of his throat almost immediately, the metallic-bleach flavor that made him gag and convinced him something was entering his body that he could not stop. In the confusion, staff were coughing, a guest was shouting, and Sokha could not tell who had been exposed or how serious it was. What stayed with him most was the sensation that his own body had betrayed him in the very moment he needed it; he has come away certain that he cannot trust his body to warn him properly or protect him, and with a broader feeling that bad things can happen to him without any way to prevent them.

In the weeks after, those beliefs hardened rather than fading. If he felt a dryness in his throat, a change in his breathing, or a strange taste while drinking coffee, he took it as proof that his body was unreliable and that danger could already be underway before he understood it. Because he had come to believe he could not stop bad things from happening, he began checking himself repeatedly for signs of injury or exposure, pressing at his throat, noticing his breathing, scanning for any sensation that might mean the chemicals had done lasting damage. The same beliefs spread outward into how he moved through the hotel. He watched hallways, housekeeping carts, maintenance closets, and the expressions on staff faces for signs that something was wrong. He also pulled away from reminders, cutting off conversations when employees mentioned the spill or later safety changes, because being reminded of it felt less like remembering and more like being returned to a moment in which he was helpless again.

The memories themselves have remained unusually immediate. He does not simply think about the exposure; at unpredictable moments the memory forces itself into his mind, and when it does he can taste that same chemical bitterness as if it is on his tongue again. Standing near the laundry room at work, catching the smell of industrial cleaners, or hearing a guest complain that a room smells “too strong” can make him feel, for a few seconds, as though the event is happening right now. Those moments have reinforced his conviction that his body cannot be trusted and that he is not really at home anywhere anymore. He says the hotel used to feel like his place, but now every back corridor and supply room can turn unfamiliar in an instant, and even at home he feels set apart, as if he no longer belongs in ordinary life with people who are not braced for something toxic to happen.

Because the memories arrive so forcefully, he has become more vigilant and more avoidant over time. When an intrusive image or the chemical taste comes back during a shift, he starts checking the air vents, looking for leaks, watching staff movements, and monitoring his chest and throat. He may reroute himself away from the service areas for the rest of the day or abruptly end a discussion if someone starts revisiting the incident. These habits give him brief relief, but they also keep his attention fixed on signs of threat. The more he scans his body and surroundings, the more easily normal sensations or small delays become loaded with danger; if housekeeping is late answering a radio call, he is quick to assume something bad has happened. Once that fear spikes, his body goes tense and ready, and in that state the memory becomes even easier to trigger. A routine pause outside a chemical storage room can bring back the taste, the panic, and the sense of being trapped in the original exposure.

Over months, this has tightened into a daily pattern. His body feels constantly on alert, and false alarms are frequent; a harmless smell, a cough from a staff member, or a late response over the hotel radio can make him react as if there is an immediate emergency. That alarm then confirms, in his mind, that he was right not to trust his body or the world around him. He becomes more certain that he cannot prevent bad things, more convinced that he does not belong in spaces other people move through casually, and more dependent on checking, scanning, and shutting down reminders. At work this has changed how he manages. Staff have noticed that he hovers near maintenance issues, repeatedly asks whether anyone feels dizzy or unwell, and avoids longer debriefs about safety procedures if they come too close to the day of the spill. At home, his partner sees him go quiet after certain smells or after delays that other people would dismiss, and then watch his own breathing for long stretches.

By the time he sought help, Sokha was exhausted by how quickly an ordinary workday could become a scene of danger in his mind and body. What finally pushed him into treatment was realizing that a minor cleaning complaint from a guest had left him shaking, tasting the chemicals again, and unable to finish the conversation without stepping out to check himself in the mirror. He is frightened that this will keep shrinking his life and his work until there is nowhere he feels safe or at ease. At the same time, he is hoping that treatment might help him trust his body enough to stop living as if another exposure is always about to happen.
